title: Vietnamese Zen
hookLine: the Truc Lam school founded by a king who became a monk

lines: UP THE MOUNTAIN OF YEN TU.
cards: A crown, set down on a table. Royal robes, folded. A king has held his country together through war, and has a son ready to rule.
Instead of staying on the throne until the end, he hands it over. In time he puts on a monk's plain robe and climbs a mountain called Yen Tu, in the north of Vietnam.
There, among the trees, he starts a school of Zen named for a bamboo grove.

teach.b: The meditation school we met in China as Chan, in Korea as Seon, and in Japan as Zen, is called Thien in Vietnam. All of these names go back to the Sanskrit word for meditation, dhyana.
Thien had already been in Vietnam a long while, in several lines of teachers, before our king.

teach.h: TRAN NHAN TONG GIVES UP THE THRONE.
teach.b: His name was Tran Nhan Tong. Vietnamese histories remember him as a ruler who led his kingdom through hard years of war, then gave the throne to his son while he was still able to rule.
Some years later he became a monk on Mount Yen Tu, and there he founded the Truc Lam school.
Truc Lam means bamboo grove. It gathered Vietnam's lines of Thien into one, a school that was Vietnam's own, and its teaching was direct.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA IN YOUR OWN HEART.
teach.b: Verses attributed to the king say that the Buddha is not somewhere far away, but in your own heart, and that you can practice the Way while living in the world: working, eating, resting.
When the mind is quiet, everyday life becomes the practice.
The school honors him as its first patriarch, and the pagodas of Yen Tu still draw pilgrims up the mountain. The point isn't that everyone should leave everything.
It's that he did leave something, and in the story, less was enough.

how: Vietnamese Buddhists honor Tran Nhan Tong as the founder of the Truc Lam school of Thien; pilgrims climb Mount Yen Tu to its pagodas, and Truc Lam monasteries teach seated meditation alongside everyday mindful work.

games.q: you're the king. the war is over, your son is ready to rule, and you still could. what do you do?
o: stay on the throne to the end.
hand over the throne and become a monk on a mountain.
rule and meditate in the palace.
games.why: Tran Nhan Tong gave the throne to his son, became a monk on Mount Yen Tu, and founded the Truc Lam school.

practice: Think of your day as a room with too much in it, and look around slowly for one thing you could set down, the way the king set down his crown: a worry you keep picking up, one errand, one extra yes.
Don't do anything about it yet; just imagine putting it on the table. Then rest with the breath, a little lighter.
